title: Math Class Asks Kids to Become Somebody Else
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer argues that math class routinely requires students to dissociate from their rational instincts in order to be marked correct—his central example being a word problem that penalizes students for giving the exact right answer in favor of an estimation the teacher wanted. The problem is not incidental but structural: math pedagogy asks kids to suspend disbelief at contrived scenarios, accept arbitrary rules over their better judgment, and perform a kind of compliance theater hundreds of times per year. Meyer traces this to an ethical failure in how problem designers treat students: the teacher is rewarded for getting kids to estimate, not for genuinely respecting kids' mathematical instincts, so students become objects in service of a pedagogical project rather than subjects with their own rational minds. His prescription is to build contexts where mathematical thinking feels natural and necessary—his 'Moley Goalie' example creates a situation where estimation is genuinely useful because the answer constraints require it—taking students as they are and building from there. The alternative, inviting students daily to choose between themselves and mathematics, produces the predictable result: they choose themselves.
points: Math class asks students to disassociate from their rational instincts hundreds of times per year—accepting wrong answers as right, suspending disbelief at contrived scenarios, treating precision as a flaw when imprecision is desired.

The underlying ethical failure is that teachers are rewarded for getting students to perform a behavior (estimating), not for creating conditions where that behavior feels genuinely necessary and natural.

Treating students as objects in service of a pedagogical project—rather than as subjects with their own rational minds—is the mechanism that drives students to feel they must become somebody else to succeed in math.

Well-designed problems make mathematical thinking feel necessary: Meyer's 'Moley Goalie' example creates a context where estimation is genuinely profitable because the answer can only be given in increments of 100.
The alternative to designing for authentic mathematical engagement is to invite students daily to choose between themselves and mathematics—and then be surprised when they choose themselves.
quotes: Students frequently feel like they have to leave essential parts of themselves at the classroom door in order to be successful in math class.

Then the student has to somehow metabolize the fact that they are marked incorrect by their teacher for answering with the exact answer and not an inexact answer. Success in this problem requires imprecision even when precision is right there. You're right if you're wrong.

Math class asks kids to disassociate from their better selves and rational instincts hundreds of times throughout a school year. Kids realize quickly that there is zero upside in asking 'okay but is there a situation where estimation is actually useful?'

The teacher is rewarded for getting the kid to estimate, not for getting the kid to inhabit themselves more fully. The teacher then treats the kid as an object in service of that project, rather than their own subject.
We can ask ourselves, 'What is a situation where estimation might feel necessary and natural? If estimation is aspirin, then what is the headache?'

This activity, like all others in our curriculum, comes from an ethic that says, 'How can we take kids as they are and build from there, to build better versions of ourselves together?' The alternative is to ask kids daily to become somebody else, to invite them to choose daily between themselves and mathematics. Their choice shouldn't surprise us.
